rationale: The book's identification — 'the heart of the earth' is Jerusalem, the navel/heart of the land — is directly attested by the only scriptural texts that speak in the phrase's own idiom: Ezekiel 5:5 ('This is Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations') and Ezekiel 38:12/Judges 9:37 (tabbur ha'aretz, the navel of the land). No Scripture ever calls a grave or tomb the 'heart of the earth,' so the dominant tomb reading rests on inference from the burial narratives rather than on any lexical parallel. The book supplies a genuine intra-scriptural mirror: Jonah's own prayer locates him 'in the heart of the seas' (bilvav yammim, Jonah 2:3, flattened to 'midst' in the KJV), and given the accepted premise that the sea is the mass of peoples over which the ship of state rides (prior Ship finding, FULL), the heart of the seas is the center of the nations — making 'heart of the earth/land' its exact counterpart, the city God set in the midst of the nations. The Jerusalem reading also resolves the notorious counting problem without idiom-rescue: seized on the night of betrayal, out on the third day, matching Luke 24:21 ('to day is the third day since these things were done,' where 'these things' include the arrest and trial, not only the burial). The strongest counter (tomb/Sheol) maps the containment structure of the analogy naturally and can invoke Jonah 2:2 ('belly of Sheol') and Acts 2:27, but the book explains those same texts within its reading — death, burial, and Sheol fall inside the three days under the swallowing power's custody, and the tomb itself was sealed and guarded by Jerusalem's authority — whereas the counter cannot connect Ezekiel 5:5 or 38:12 to Matthew 12:40 at all and must defend its chronology by appeal to inclusive-counting idiom. No supplied text is explained by the counter that the book's core cannot explain without contradiction, so under the comparative standard the book prevails.
book_core_identification: 'The heart of the earth' in Matthew 12:40 is Jerusalem — the city Scripture locates as the navel and heart of the land, set in the midst of the nations (Ezek 5:5; 38:12) — so the Son of Man's three days and three nights are measured under Jerusalem's power, from His seizure on the night of betrayal to His coming out on the third day, rather than denoting the tomb or Hades as such.
book_secondary_elaborations: The count of three days and three nights begins at the arrest outside the gates, resolving the Friday-to-Sunday counting problem (Luke 24:13, 21)
The great fish is the devouring ruler — Caesar/Rome — acting through the sea of peoples (Jer 51:34, 44; Ezek 29:3; 32:2; John 19:15)

The whole book of Jonah is a scene-by-scene prophecy of the Passion: the flight/Judas, the storm/the rulers' fear of Rome, the interrogation/Pilate, the casting/Caiaphas's bargain, the sailors' worship/the centurion, the reeds/the crown of thorns, Nineveh's repentance/the gospel to the nations, Jonah's anger/Israel's envy
Extra-biblical corroboration that Jerusalem was known as the heart/navel of the earth (Philo, Sibylline Oracles, Greek Ezekiel variants)
Death, burial, and Sheol are contained within the three days as events inside the swallowing power's dominion, not the referent of the phrase itself
Nineveh's three days' journey read as three thousand years via the day-as-thousand-years scale (2 Pet 3:8)
strongest_counter_interpretation: 'The heart of the earth' means the grave/tomb and, in the traditional extension, Sheol/Hades: as Jonah was contained inside the fish's belly — which he himself calls 'the belly of Sheol' (Jonah 2:2) — so Jesus was contained inside the earth, buried in the tomb (Matt 27:57-60) and in the realm of the dead (Acts 2:27-31; Ps 16:10; Eph 4:9), from His death until His resurrection on the third day; 'three days and three nights' is Hebrew inclusive-counting idiom (cf. Esther 4:16 with 5:1; 1 Sam 30:12-13) and poses no real chronological difficulty.
counter_core_identification: The heart of the earth is the grave/Sheol — the interior of the earth where Jesus' body lay and His soul sojourned between death and resurrection.
material_core_denial: If 'the heart of the earth' denotes the tomb/Sheol entered only at death, then it cannot denote Jerusalem entered at the arrest: the two readings assign the phrase different referents, different starting points for the three-day count, and different locations (inside the ground versus within the city's power), and both cannot be true of the same referent.
counter_case: Matthew's analogy structurally pairs containment with containment: 'in the whale's belly' parallels 'in the heart of the earth,' which most naturally means inside the earth — burial — not presence in a city

Jonah himself names his location Sheol: 'out of the belly of hell cried I' (Jonah 2:2), and Peter applies Psalm 16:10 ('not leave my soul in hell... nor suffer thine Holy One to see corruption') to Christ's death interval (Acts 2:27-31), anchoring the antitype in the realm of the dead
Ephesians 4:9 ('he descended into the lower parts of the earth') and 1 Peter 3:18-19 supply a traditional descent-to-the-dead frame matching a subterranean referent
1 Corinthians 15:3-4 ('buried... raised on the third day') ties the three-day sign to burial, and the burial narratives (Matt 27:57-60) supply an obvious referent
The chronological objection dissolves under Hebrew inclusive counting (Esther 4:16/5:1; Gen 42:17-18), so the counting problem does not force relocating the referent
Jesus suffered and was buried outside the city wall (Heb 13:12; John 19:41), which strains a strictly 'in Jerusalem' reading
book_explanatory_advantages: Scripture explicitly calls Jerusalem the city set 'in the midst of the nations' (Ezek 5:5) and the people at 'the midst/navel of the land' — tabbur ha'aretz (Ezek 38:12; Judg 9:37) — while no Scripture ever calls a grave the 'heart of the earth'

Jonah's own prayer contains the mirrored phrase 'in the heart of the seas' (bilvav yammim, Jonah 2:3), and with the accepted premise that the sea is the peoples borne under the ship of state, heart-of-seas = center of the nations, making heart-of-earth = the land's center by exact parallel within the very typology Jesus cites
The reading resolves 'three days and three nights' exactly — seized Thursday night, out Sunday, matching Luke 24:21's 'third day since these things were done' — without appeal to counting idiom

The great-fish mechanics cohere: Scripture names devouring rulers as swallowers who must give back (Jer 51:34, 44; Ezek 29:3; 32:2), matching Rome/Caesar named at the sentence (John 19:15) and the ship-of-state bargain of Caiaphas (John 11:48-50), consistent with the prior adjudicated Ship symbol

The scene-by-scene Jonah–Passion correspondence (flight/Judas, sleeper/Gethsemane, interrogation/Pilate, hand-washing, casting, gentile worship, mission to the nations) is explained only if the sign spans the whole custody, not merely the entombment
Contemporary usage confirms recognizability: Philo calls Jerusalem the 'heart of the whole earth,' the Sibylline Oracles 'the navel and heart of the earth'

The book's reading contains the counter's data rather than denying it: death, burial, and Sheol fall inside the three days under the swallowing power, and Jonah's Sheol-language ('as good as dead,' alive and praying) fits a man in the dominion of the devourer, not a corpse in a grave
counter_explanatory_advantages: Direct containment parallel (belly ↔ interior of the earth) is the most natural surface reading of Matthew 12:40
Jonah 2:2's 'belly of Sheol' and Acts 2:27-31 give the death/Sheol referent explicit scriptural language within the same typology
It aligns with 1 Cor 15:3-4's burial-and-third-day formula and the burial narratives without requiring gē to mean 'land' or a custody-based extension of 'in Jerusalem'
It represents the near-unanimous historical reading across traditions
decisive_sources: Ezekiel 5:5 — God's own declaration that Jerusalem is set in the midst of the nations
Ezekiel 38:12 with Judges 9:37 — tabbur ha'aretz, the navel of the land, flattened to 'midst' in the KJV
Jonah 2:3 (Hebrew bilvav yammim, 'in the heart of the seas') — the mirrored phrase inside the cited sign
Revelation 17:15 with the prior Ship finding — the sea as peoples/nations, fixing the scale of 'heart of the seas'
Luke 24:13, 21 — 'to day is the third day since these things were done,' anchoring the count to the arrest-to-resurrection interval
Jeremiah 51:34, 44 — the devouring ruler forced to disgorge what he swallowed, supplying the fish's mechanics
John 11:48-50 and 19:15 — the ship-of-state bargain and the naming of Caesar, locating the swallowing power
Philo and the Sibylline Oracles — contemporary attestation of 'heart/navel of the earth' as Jerusalem's epithet
unresolved_objections: Matthew's analogy pairs 'belly of the whale' with 'heart of the earth,' and Jonah calls that belly 'the belly of Sheol' (Jonah 2:2), which the tomb/Sheol reading maps more directly than the Jerusalem reading
The chronological argument is weakened if 'three days and three nights' is inclusive-counting idiom (Esther 4:16/5:1), removing one motive for relocating the referent
Jesus was condemned, crucified, and buried outside the city wall, so 'in Jerusalem' requires the custody-of-the-polity extension rather than literal presence within the city
The secondary day-as-thousand-years reading of Nineveh's three days' journey is asserted, not demonstrated, in the supplied material
